title: We need to distinguish between the Ludlumist and the Damonic ways of looking at adaptations.

commenti.body:
I think this isn't really needed because movie watchers don't watch movies to judge the strictness of the adaptation, but the quality of the storytelling. And the original install base of the adaptation is just a tiny fraction of the wider audience for a movie.

The Watsonian vs Doylist debate grew out of interpretation of text. Those inherently are trying to dissect meaning from the exact same thing and engaging with the same material on a fairly consistent level. So different perspectives become valuable and can grow out of their own.

But a movie is usually judged on quality alone because a movie is serving a different audience than the source material.

Take the Marvel Movies. As faithful adaptations, they are failures. But no one cares except for a small contingent of fans that actually read comics (which is getting smaller by the day). Because the audience for a marvel movie is massive and outnumbers the original fans 1000 to 1.

So I think we can simply get by saying X is a faithful adaptation and Y is an unfaithful adaptation. Because that tells you everything you need to know. Saying something is Damonic (which shouldn't it be Limanist or Greengrassic?) or Ludlumist just obfuscates the original point which is clarifying how faithful an adaptation is.

I agree with the notion that those are the two camps of thought. Although maybe in need of more universal terms, like Textualist (Ludlumist) and Transformalist (Damonic). Plot heavy novels really do lend themselves to more of a direct adaptation rather than more transformative take, but neither is always the right answer.

As the years pass, I think it's clear that they should have followed the books more because they really mined that well dry in terms of their "original" story. Every movie was a carbon copy of the first. The new CIA boss, who was the real mastermind of Treadstone, decides it's time to finally get rid of Bourne once and for all. 

And then the next movie, well, turns out that wasn't the super final head of Treadstone, here they are now, and this time, they are finally going to get rid of Bourne for good. Honest this time....I mean...there couldn't actually be a different, even higher up boss for the next movie, right? And all of this for Bourne to once again unlock a single memory. 

First one is the only one I can revisit.
Fr, like Damon didn’t even write this even if we wanted to do microcosmic terminology for no reason lol

You seem naive in your description of how "most people" watch things

I certainly agree with you about how people *should* judge movies, but there are a lot of people who care very deeply about faithfulness of adaptation, and it's often difficult to avoid that perspective when discussing certain works. You can avoid it by only ever talking to fellow cinephiles, but sometimes you want to talk to normal people about movies and this comes up.

The way I currently deal with this is roughly how you do: by dismissing anyone who cares primarily about the Ludlumian perspective as misguided, obsessed with niche issues that no one cares about

The value of the Ludlumian/Damonist distinction is that it emphasizes how this alternate perspective isn't simply borne of ignorance, it's a legitimate way to view the world. The whole point of the shift, from my perspective, would be to be less condescending when talking to normies

I mean the reason I view it that way is because that's just how media works. 

Just look at the Bourne identity book vs movie.

In 1980, the year the book came out, it sold 325000 copies. Assuming every person that bought the book read it, that is 325,000 people who have read the book


The movie in 2002 made $214 million. At $10 dollars a movie ticket (which would be quite the price in 2002), that is 21 million people watching the movie.

Of course more people could have read the book on loan or from the library.

But more people could have watched the movie on DVD post haste or seen it at a discount.

So no matter what, the size of the films audience is a magnitude larger than the size of the books audience.

In the simplest terms, the vast majority of the films audience won't care about the faithfulness of an adaptation because they will literally have never read the book for comparison.

And that goes for nearly any adaptation. The adaptation almost always has a much much larger install base than the original.

So faithfulness is just a trite critique from a specific subsection of the audience that really doesn't impact the end product.

The only time faithfulness comes into question is when the adaptation is already a lackluster story.

Nobody cares about the faithfulness of Jurassic Park, even thought it takes several huge liberties from the chrichton book, because it's a phenomenal movie and anybody that would actually criticize the faithfulness will be drowned out by the masses.

Or for a more recent example, Oppenheimer, which is drastically different than American Prometheus but still immensely praised.

People care about the faithfulness of say Percy Jackson and the Olympians, cause the movies sucked, and the loudest critics rise to the top of the complainers.

So unless you are only talking to people that watch adaptations of works they have already consumed, this shouldn't be an issue.
